newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen acquisition may help sweeten offer.
newsitem.headline: Loewen acquisition may help sweeten offer.

text.p: Loewen Group Inc's move through a joint venture to acquire Rose Hills Co Inc may play a role in getting a sweeter offer from suitor Service Corp International, analysts said on Friday.

Vancouver-based Loewen is teaming up with merchant bank Blackstone Group to buy the cemetery and mortuary operations and assets of Rose Hills Co and The Rose Hill Memorial Park Association for US$240 million.
Loewen said the Rose Hill deal was in the works well before Service Corp launched its US$43 a share bid on Tuesday.

"I'm hard-pressed to think from any standpoint that this is negative. It's good for Loewen on its own and it's good for Service if it wins the day," said David Brodie, an analyst with CIBC Wood Gundy.

Loewen will get an immediate earnings boost from the Rose Hill deal and has the option to acquire Blackstone's majority stake in the venture in four years. Loewen and Blackstone were in a similar deal last June to acquire Prime Succession Inc, the largest privately owned funeral home operator in the United States, for US$320 million. Brodie said Loewen could use the promise of future growth to keep shareholders on side.
"They could say, 'These things are going to kick in with a good return four years down the road, so we've got extra future growth, so stick with us,'" Brodie said.

Assuming that the deal was structured similar to the Prime Succession venture, the Rose Hill deal would give Loewen a call option on future business for a reasonable amount of upfront capital, another analyst said.
"It does to a degree solidify the future without essentially paying for it right now," the analyst said.
But Rose Hill could also make Loewen more attractive to Service Corp, rumored to be a rival bidder for Rose Hill.
"Ironically, to the extent that it is positive (for Loewen), it makes Loewen even that much more attractive to Service Corp," Brodie said.
Meanwhile, Loewen chief financial officer Paul Wagler has said the board of directors will meet in the next few days to decide whether to fight the bid.
Blackstone officials said on Friday that they had not been approached by Loewen to help mount a defense.
"We're nowhere near to talking about what our role would be, if any, if they decided to launch any kind of defense," Blackstone Capital Partners spokesman Howard Lipson said.
"Other than to say, 'Look guys, we think you're terrific. If your plans call for something that involves private equity, we hope you think of us,' and I know they would," Lipson said.
Loewen stock closed down 0.60 at 57.40 on 564,000 shares on Friday on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
On Nasdaq, the stock dropped 3/8 to 42 on 966,000 shares.
